topComments.author: akoboldfrying
topComments.text: Always cool to see this come up. I really like the idea of "encoding" the video as... x86 machine instructions! The hairsplitting nerd in me can't help but point out that the claim in the Part 2 article that the problem of combining deltas is NP hard isn't true. In fact you can solve this optimally in O(n^3) time with DP: Let g(i, j) be the minimum number of bytes needed to encode input deltas i..j as a single (i.e., combined) output delta. Given g(i, j), computing g(i, j+1) takes constant time, so we can compute all of this function's values in O(n^2) total time. Now let f(i, j) be the minimum number of bytes needed to encode input deltas i..j using any sequence of output deltas (combined or not). Note that any such sequence must consist of some number (possibly zero) of optimally encoded output deltas followed by an optimally encoded output delta that itself ends with input delta j. IOW, it must be that f(i, j) is equal to f(i, k) + g(k+1, j) for some k, and there are at most n values of k that we need to try, so we can compute each value of f() in O(n); there are O(n^2) values to compute, so O(n^3) time overall. f(1, n) is then the minimum number of bytes needed to encode the entire list of input deltas, and standard backtracing through the DP matrix can be used to recover the actual sequence of output deltas.

topComments.text: My advice is not specific to Matrix but other self hosted private services. Some of this may or may not be feasible with Matrix. (I have never used Matrix) - Whether family or friends, always suggest it as a "fallback" for when "preferred service" is down and to use when discussion ultra-sensitive topics or sharing financial files. With time they may just stay connected to it if the friction to do so is low. It has to be their choice, not yours. - What helps? Add more incentives such as perks that "preferred service" does not offer. No file size limits. No or few file type limits. No content filters. Add emoji's or gifs that align with their inside jokes and their style of humor. Keeping random people away is very important. Making your friends and family administrators or moderators and let them decide how it operates. Do not moderate or power-trip over your friends or family or they will leave. Limit rules to "Do not break the laws of this country in public chatrooms" and private chat rooms if you do not physically host the server . Database and file backups become even more important but they will feel in control of a thing. Have a keyword or code word they all learn means to go check the private platform that "primary platform" would not recognize. Maybe when they see "Turtle Farts!" they know to go log into your service. - They may just stay on their primary preferred service. Every group is different and not every group will see the benefits of your fallback service. They may not appreciate the work you put into setting it up for them. Do not expect to get the friends of your friends and family to move to your service. They may not appreciate the OpSec value until "Bad Things"(c)™2038 happen to enough people. Just be there for when it does. - If there are concerns that you would spy on them, consider instead using eJapperd or Prosody as you can implement OMEMO for individual and group end-to-end encrypted messages. stackOverflowQuestions.title: OkHttp HTTP/2 writeTimeout when server sets INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE to 4096: Http2Writer.dataFrame does not call sink.flush()
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: Problem Summary When communicating with an HTTP/2 server that advertises a small SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE (e.g., 4096 ), OkHttp fails to send request body data, resulting in a writeTimeout / SocketTimeoutException . Traffic captures confirm that no TCP TX occurs from the client, meaning the data remains buffered locally. I have traced this to Http2Writer.dataFrame() , which (unlike settings() , ping() , goAway() , and other writer methods) does not call sink.flush() after writing the frame payload. The debug logger prints the frame as if it were sent, but the bytes stay in the buffer. If the server uses the default INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE of 65535 , the request data is transmitted successfully and everything works as expected. Environment OkHttp: 5.5.1 Protocol: HTTP/2 (h2) Steps to Reproduce Connect to an HTTP/2 server that advertises SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE = 4096 (or any value smaller than the request body size). Send a request with a body larger than the advertised window. Observe that OkHttp writes a DATA frame of size 4096 , the logger emits >> 0x00000003 4096 DATA , but no writeTimeout occurs eventually because the bytes are never flushed to the socket. The server never receives the data and never sends WINDOW_UPDATE , so the client eventually times out. Expected Behavior The DATA frame payload should be flushed to the underlying sink (similar to other frame types), allowing the TCP stack to transmit the bytes and the server to acknowledge receipt with WINDOW_UPDATE . Actual Behavior The bytes remain in Okio's RealBufferedSink buffer. The debug log misleadingly shows the frame as "sent." No network transmission occurs. writeTimeout fires after the configured timeout. Workaround (Confirmed) Adding sink.flush() after sink.write(buffer!!, byteCount.toLong()) inside Http2Writer.dataFrame() resolves the issue immediately. Possible Root Cause in BufferedSink ? It is worth considering whether the problem originates not in Http2Writer itself but in the behavior

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Benchmarking Python Decorator Overhead
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I am working on the project Type Enforced which is a framework for enforcing python type hints using a decorator. I am trying to benchmark this project vs other fast frameworks like Beartype. Essentially, the overhead for initializing a function is far greater than the overhead of adding the decorator. In this sense, I have been taking the differential of execution time between the decorated function time and the undecorated function time averages. Now, these differential measurements are falling at about 10 ns for Type Enforced vs about 200 ns for Beartype on basic validations like: def my_fn_vanilla(a:int): pass @type_enforced.Enforcer def my_fn_te(a:int): pass @beartype def my_fn_bt(a:int): pass Essentially, I run each of these functions n times and take the average time of running them. I then subtract the average of n runs for: te_diff = avg_time_my_fn_te - avg_time_my_fn_vanilla bt_diff = avg_time_my_fn_bt - avg_time_my_fn_vanilla Such that I can compare the additional apples to apples on added overhead since just running the vanilla function takes about 5000 ns while the added overhead for type_enforced and beartype are about 10 ns and 200 ns respectively. These timings are pretty stable at smaller and larger sizes of timing samples and across system architectures (relative to processor and memory yada yada - but still relative on orders of magnitude). My concern stems from the fact that we are measuring python in terms of 20 clock cycles of differential. Assuming there are no bug in the code or measurements, is this something that can be trusted? I am looking for some holes in the methodology that I should be checking for and potential edge cases I may be missing. Are there documented other ways that this can be measured / benchmarked / tested? Related to a previous post: https://codereview.stackexchange.com/questions/302938/benchmarking-type-hint-validation-in-python/302948#302948 . stackOverflowQuestions.title: Calculate dependent due dates for Activity B based on Activity A cycles without resetting prematurely

Here is how the logic needs to work: Activity A (the base cycle) I find the latest date for Activity A per ep_Id using a ranking window function ( RANK() or ROW_NUMBER() ) The next due date is calculated by adding 6 months to this latest date using DATEADD Once this 6-month due date is completed, it becomes the new "latest" date for the next cycle Activity B (the dependent cycle) Activity B is also tracked by ep_Id Its next due date should be calculated as 6 months + 90 days (essentially 90 days after the corresponding Activity A 6-month due date) The catch: Activity B's due date must remain static. It should not automatically reset or shift whenever a new Activity A cycle rolls over or gets completed. It needs to stay locked in until Activity B itself is actually completed on its 90th due date How can I write a SQL query or CTE structure to properly maintain this static offset for Activity B while allowing Activity A to roll over independently. stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I am designing a class similar to an std::array . I have a constructor that receives an iterator and a size. My idea is fail if the size is bigger than N . Code: constexpr vector_stack_base(const_iterator source, size_type count) { if consteval { static_assert(N <= count); } else { if (count > N) { count = N; } } This codes fails in MSVC 2026, in C++23 in the static_assert , saying: "error C2131: expression did not evaluate to a constant". Of course, count is not const, but given the if consteval we are in a constant evaluated context, so count must be a compile time constant. I know I can design it in a different way like having count as a non type template parameter and then, this function overloaded for runtime, but I think this is a case for consteval, but I do not know what count is not considered constatn in a consteval if branch. infoqArticles.description: Tiger Data has released pg_vectorsearch, an open source PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity search, currently in alpha. infoqArticles.author: Renato Losio

infoqArticles.title: Varlock Releases Bumpy: A File-Based Versioning Alternative to Changesets
infoqArticles.description: Bumpy is an MIT-licensed, TypeScript tool for version management and changelogs in monorepos. It follows the changesets workflow, using markdown bump files, and adds support for workspace and catalog protocols, custom publish commands, and branch-based prereleases. Changesets v3, released in August 2026, closed many earlier gaps, though differences remain. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Yelp Combines Native and Server-Driven UI for Its AI Assistant
infoqArticles.description: Yelp combines native mobile controls with server-driven conversation rendering in its AI Assistant using the CHAOS framework. The architecture separates view configuration from conversation data, supports backend-driven chat interactions, and enables faster UI updates without new app releases. Yelp also discusses cross-platform challenges and reuse for its Biz Ask Anything pilot. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: GitLab 19.5 Makes Agentic Development a Governed Part of the DevOps Platform

infoqArticles.title: TypeScript 7.1 Beta: Restores the Compiler API and Makes Vue and Svelte First-Class
infoqArticles.description: TypeScript 7.1 Beta, announced October 20, 2026, restores the compiler API removed in 7.0, now split into separate entry points. It adds content mappers, letting tools like Vue check non-standard files. One Vue project's type checks fell from 14.19 to 3.10 seconds. An editor issue remains open, and teams may need TypeScript 6 alongside 7. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis
